text: The available evidence on vitamin D and mortality was considered inconclusive. The review aimed to assess the beneficial and harmful effects of vitamin D for prevention of mortality in adults.

The authors searched multiple databases and included randomized trials comparing vitamin D at any dose, duration, and route of administration versus placebo or no intervention. Vitamin D could be administered as vitamin D3, vitamin D2, alfacalcidol, or calcitriol.
Six authors extracted data independently. Random-effects and fixed-effect meta-analyses were conducted, and trial sequential analyses were used to minimize the risk of random errors.

Fifty randomized trials with 94,148 participants provided mortality data. Most trials included elderly women older than 70 years, and vitamin D was administered for a median of two years. Overall, vitamin D decreased mortality slightly.

When different forms of vitamin D were assessed separately, only vitamin D3 decreased mortality significantly, whereas vitamin D2, alfacalcidol, and calcitriol did not. Vitamin D3 combined with calcium significantly increased nephrolithiasis. Alfacalcidol and calcitriol significantly increased hypercalcaemia.

When different forms of vitamin D were assessed separately, only vitamin D3 decreased mortality significantly, whereas vitamin D2, alfacalcidol, and calcitriol did not. Vitamin D3 without calcium significantly increased nephrolithiasis. Alfacalcidol and calcitriol significantly increased hypercalcaemia.

Secretory immunoglobulin A acts as the first line of adaptive humoral immune defense at mucosal surfaces. A lack of SIgA or the inability to produce antigen-specific SIgA can increase the risk of infections. Dietary intake may improve mucosal immunity by accelerating SIgA secretion.

This study investigated the effect of dietary intake of Agaricus bisporus white button mushroom on salivary IgA secretion in healthy subjects. Twenty-four healthy volunteers were randomly assigned to a normal daily diet or a normal diet with WBM. The active group consumed 100 g of blanched WBM daily with their normal diet for one week, whereas the control group consumed their normal diet without WBM.
Saliva was collected before and after commencement of the study and every week thereafter for three weeks. Saliva flow rate, sIgA concentration, and osmolality were determined.

There was no significant difference between pre- and postdietary mushroom intakes for all indices in the control group. In contrast, the mean sIgA secretion rate increased significantly at weeks 1 and 2 in the WBM intake group and then returned to baseline at week 3.

Changes in sIgA secretion rate over the intervention period were greater in the WBM group than in the control group without WBM. No significant changes in osmolality and saliva IgG were noted in either group. The dietary intake of A. bisporus WBM significantly accelerated sIgA secretion, indicating potential health benefits for improving mucosal immunity.
Saliva was collected before and after commencement of the study and every week thereafter for three weeks. Saliva flow rate and sIgA concentration were determined, excluding osmolality.

The study compared the effects of calorie-restricted vegetarian and conventional diabetic diets, alone and in combination with exercise, on insulin resistance, visceral fat, and oxidative stress markers in subjects with Type 2 diabetes.

A 24-week randomized open parallel design was used. Seventy-four patients with Type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to either a vegetarian diet or a conventional diabetic diet. Both diets were isocaloric and calorie restricted. The second 12 weeks of the diet were combined with aerobic exercise.

Primary outcomes included insulin sensitivity measured by hyperinsulinaemic isoglycaemic clamp, visceral and subcutaneous fat volume measured by magnetic resonance imaging, and oxidative stress measured by thiobarbituric acid reactive substances.

Compared with the conventional diabetic diet, the vegetarian diet produced greater reductions in diabetes medication, body weight, visceral fat, and subcutaneous fat. Insulin sensitivity increased more in the vegetarian diet group than in the conventional diet group.

Plasma adiponectin increased and leptin decreased in the vegetarian diet group, while vitamin C, superoxide dismutase, and reduced glutathione also increased. Differences between groups were greater after the addition of exercise training, and changes in insulin sensitivity and enzymatic oxidative stress markers correlated with changes in visceral fat.

Primary outcomes included insulin sensitivity measured by hyperinsulinaemic isoglycaemic clamp, visceral and subcutaneous fat volume measured by magnetic resonance imaging, and oxidative stress measured without thiobarbituric acid reactive substances.

Antibiotics alter the microbial balance within the gastrointestinal tract. Probiotics may prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea by restoring the gut microflora. Antibiotics are prescribed frequently in children, and antibiotic-associated diarrhea is common in this population.

The review assessed the efficacy and adverse effects of probiotics for preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhea in children. It also assessed adverse events associated with probiotics when co-administered with antibiotics in children.

Randomized parallel controlled trials were eligible if they compared co-administered probiotics with antibiotics for preventing diarrhea secondary to antibiotic use in children aged 0 to 18 years. Dichotomous outcomes included incidence of diarrhea and adverse events, while continuous outcomes included mean duration of diarrhea and mean daily stool frequency.

Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Trials included treatment with Lactobacilli species, Bifidobacterium species, Streptococcus species, or Saccharomyces boulardii alone or in combination. Six studies used a single-strain probiotic agent and four studies combined two probiotic strains.

Per protocol analysis showed statistically significant results favoring probiotics over controls, but intention-to-treat analysis was not significant overall. Five of ten trials monitored adverse events, and none reported a serious adverse event. The authors concluded that probiotics show promise for preventing pediatric antibiotic-associated diarrhea, but the evidence was not strong enough to recommend routine use.

Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Trials included treatment with Lactobacilli species, Bifidobacterium species, or Saccharomyces boulardii alone or in combination, excluding Streptococcus species. Six studies used a single-strain probiotic agent and four studies combined two probiotic strains.

Standard therapies for antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea have limited efficacy. Probiotic prophylaxis was presented as a promising alternative for reducing the incidence of both AAD and CDAD.

In this single-center randomized double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging study, 255 adult inpatients were randomized to Pro-2, Pro-1, or placebo. Pro-2 received two probiotic capsules per day, Pro-1 received one probiotic capsule and one placebo capsule per day, and the placebo group received two placebo capsules per day.

Each probiotic capsule contained 50 billion colony-forming units of live organisms, specifically Lactobacillus acidophilus CL1285 and Lactobacillus casei LBC80R Bio-K+ CL1285. Probiotic prophylaxis began within 36 hours of initial antibiotic administration, continued for five days after the last antibiotic dose, and patients were followed for an additional 21 days.

Pro-2 had a lower antibiotic-associated diarrhea incidence than Pro-1, and each probiotic group had a lower AAD incidence than placebo. Among patients who acquired AAD, both Pro-2 and Pro-1 had shorter symptom duration than placebo.

Pro-2 had a lower Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea incidence than Pro-1, and each treatment group had a lower CDAD incidence than placebo. Gastrointestinal symptoms were less common in the treatment groups than in placebo and in Pro-2 than in Pro-1. The probiotic blend was well tolerated and effective for reducing AAD and especially CDAD in hospitalized patients on antibiotics.

Each probiotic capsule contained 50 billion colony-forming units of live organisms, specifically Lactobacillus acidophilus CL1285, excluding Lactobacillus casei LBC80R Bio-K+ CL1285. Probiotic prophylaxis began within 36 hours of initial antibiotic administration, continued for five days after the last antibiotic dose, and patients were followed for an additional 21 days.

The study noted that little information was available on viable Toxoplasma gondii in tissues of lambs worldwide. The prevalence of T. gondii was determined in 383 lambs under one year old from Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia in the United States.

Hearts from 383 lambs were obtained from a slaughterhouse on the day of killing. Blood removed from each heart was tested for antibodies to T. gondii using the modified agglutination test. Sera were screened at 1:25, 1:50, 1:100, and 1:200 dilutions, and hearts were selected for bioassay.

Antibodies to T. gondii were found in 104 of 383 lambs. Hearts of 68 seropositive lambs were used for isolation of viable T. gondii by bioassay in cats, mice, or both. In cat bioassays, myocardium was fed to cats and cat feces were examined for shedding of T. gondii oocysts. In mouse bioassays, digested myocardium was inoculated into mice and the recipient mice were examined for T. gondii infection.

In total, 53 isolates of T. gondii were obtained from 68 seropositive lambs. Genotyping of the isolates used 10 PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism markers, including SAG1, SAG2, SAG3, BTUB, GRA6, c22-8, c29-2, L358, PK1, and Apico.

Genotyping revealed 57 strains with 15 genotypes. Four lambs had infections with two T. gondii genotypes. Twenty-six strains belonged to the clonal Type II lineage, eight strains belonged to the Type III lineage, and the remaining strains were divided into atypical genotypes. The results indicated high parasite prevalence and high genetic diversity of T. gondii in lambs.

Swine confinement buildings in eastern Canada are enclosed and equipped with modern production systems to manage waste. Bioaerosols from these buildings could be contaminated by human pathogens and antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that may colonize exposed workers.

The study analyzed bioaerosols of swine confinement buildings and nasal flora of Canadian hog producers to evaluate possible colonization with human pathogens and tetracycline-resistant bacteria. Culturable and non-culturable human pathogens and tet genes were investigated in bioaerosols from 18 barns.

The nasal passages of 35 hog producers were sampled, and DNA was extracted from calcium-alginate swabs. PCR was used to detect Campylobacter, Clostridium perfringens, Enterococcus, Escherichia coli, Yersinia enterocolitica, tetA/tetC, tetG, and ribosomal protection protein genes.

Airborne culturable Clostridium perfringens, Enterococcus, Escherichia coli, and Yersinia enterocolitica were present in the bioaerosols of multiple facilities. Aerosolized total Campylobacter, Clostridium perfringens, Enterococcus, Escherichia coli, and Yersinia enterocolitica were also detected in barn bioaerosols.

Campylobacter, Clostridium perfringens, Enterococcus, Escherichia coli, and Yersinia enterocolitica were found in the nasal flora of workers. One worker was positive for tetA/tetC genes and ten workers were positive for tetG genes. The study concluded that hog producers are exposed to aerosolized human pathogens and tetracycline-resistant bacteria that can contaminate nasal flora.

Campylobacter, Clostridium perfringens, Enterococcus, and Escherichia coli were found in the nasal flora of workers, excluding Yersinia enterocolitica. One worker was positive for tetA/tetC genes and ten workers were positive for tetG genes. The study concluded that hog producers are exposed to aerosolized human pathogens and tetracycline-resistant bacteria that can contaminate nasal flora.

Between November 2006 and May 2008, a subacute neurological syndrome affected workers from two swine abattoirs in Minnesota and Indiana. These workers had occupational exposure to aerosolised porcine brain, and the study aimed to describe the pathogenic and immunological characteristics of the illness.

Patients from the two abattoirs who presented or were referred to the Mayo Clinic with neurological symptoms were included. The investigators recorded exposure details and performed neurological, laboratory, neuroimaging, electrophysiological, pathological, and autoimmune serological assessments. Healthy controls were recruited from the community and from workers at the Minnesota plant.

Twenty-four patients were identified, including 21 from Minnesota and three from Indiana. No infectious agent that could trigger disease was identified. All patients developed polyradiculoneuropathy, which was usually sensory predominant and painful. Two patients had initial central nervous system manifestations, including transverse myelitis and meningoencephalitis.

Nerve conduction studies localized abnormalities to the most proximal and distal nerve segments. Quantitative sensory and autonomic testing revealed involvement of large and small sensory fibers and sweat fibers. MRI showed prominent abnormalities of roots and ganglia, and nerve biopsies identified mild demyelination, axonal degeneration, and perivascular inflammation.

Protein concentrations were high in the cerebrospinal fluid of most tested patients. Sera from all patients and some unaffected workplace controls had a distinctive neural-reactive IgG, while none of the community controls did. Most patients' sera contained IgG specific to myelin basic protein. The disorder was interpreted as autoimmune in origin and related to occupational exposure to multiple aerosolised porcine brain tissue antigens.

Twenty-four patients were identified, including 21 from Minnesota and three from Indiana. No infectious agent that could trigger disease was identified. All patients developed polyradiculoneuropathy, which was usually sensory predominant and painful. Two patients had initial central nervous system manifestations, including transverse myelitis, excluding meningoencephalitis.

In October 2007, a cluster of patients with a novel polyradiculoneuropathy was identified at a pork abattoir. Patients worked in the primary carcass processing area, called the warm room, and most processed severed heads at the head-table.

A case-control study was conducted at Plant A to determine risk factors for illness. A case was defined as symptoms of peripheral neuropathy with compatible electrodiagnostic testing in a pork abattoir worker. Two control groups were used: randomly selected non-ill warm-room workers and all non-ill head-table workers.

Fifteen cases were identified at Plant A, with illness onsets between May 2004 and November 2007. Cases were more likely than warm-room controls to have ever worked at the head-table, removed brains or removed muscle from the backs of heads, and worked within 0 to 10 feet of the brain removal operation.

Workers removed brains by using compressed air that liquefied brain and generated aerosolized droplets, exposing themselves and nearby workers. Eight additional cases were identified in the only two other abattoirs using this technique. The three abattoirs using this technique stopped brain removal, and no new cases were reported after 24 months of follow-up.

Cases had higher median interferon-gamma levels than controls. The novel polyradiculoneuropathy was associated with removing porcine brains with compressed air. The findings supported an autoimmune mechanism consistent with immune-mediated illnesses occurring in association with neural tissue exposure.

Workers removed brains without using compressed air, avoiding liquefaction of brain tissue and aerosolized droplets. Eight additional cases were identified in two other abattoirs using related brain removal practices. The three abattoirs using this technique stopped brain removal, and no new cases were reported after 24 months of follow-up.

Alcohol-based hand rubs are an effective means of decreasing transmission of bacterial pathogens, but alcohol is not effective against Clostridium difficile spores. The study examined retention of C. difficile spores on volunteers' hands after alcohol-based hand rub use and the subsequent transfer of these spores through physical contact.

Nontoxigenic C. difficile spores were spread on the bare palms of 10 volunteers. Three alcohol-based hand rubs and chlorhexidine soap-and-water washing were compared with plain water rubbing alone for removal of C. difficile spores.

Palmar cultures were performed before and after hand decontamination using a plate stamping method. Transferability of C. difficile after application of alcohol-based hand rub was tested by having each volunteer shake hands with an uninoculated volunteer.

Plain water rubbing reduced palmar culture counts and was used as the zero point for the other products. Compared with water washing, chlorhexidine soap washing reduced spore counts. Among the alcohol-based hand rubs, Isagel, Endure, and Purell each produced reductions in spore counts.

There were no statistically significant differences between the reductions achieved by the alcohol-based hand rubs. After alcohol-based hand rub use, handshaking transferred a mean of 30% of residual C. difficile spores to recipients' hands. The authors concluded that soap-and-water hand washing was more effective than alcohol-based hand rubs for removing C. difficile spores.

Plain water rubbing reduced palmar culture counts and was used as the zero point for the other products. Compared with water washing, chlorhexidine soap washing reduced spore counts. Among the alcohol-based hand rubs, Isagel and Endure produced reductions in spore counts, excluding Purell.

Vibrio species are a rare cause of necrotizing soft-tissue infections and primary septicemia. These infections are more likely to occur in patients with hepatic disease, diabetes, adrenal insufficiency, and immunocompromised conditions. Vibrio organisms thrive in warm seawater and are often present in raw oysters, shellfish, and other seafood.

This study examined the fulminating clinical characteristics of Vibrio vulnificus and Vibrio cholerae non-O1 soft-tissue infections and identified outcome predictors. Thirty patients with necrotizing fasciitis and sepsis caused by Vibrio species were retrospectively reviewed.

Twenty-eight patients had a history of contact with seawater or raw seafood. Eight patients had hepatic disease such as hepatitis or liver cirrhosis, seven patients had diabetes mellitus, and nine patients had hepatic dysfunction combined with diabetes mellitus. Culture studies confirmed Vibrio vulnificus in 23 patients and Vibrio cholerae non-O1 in seven patients.

Surgical debridement or immediate limb amputation was initially performed in all patients with necrotizing soft-tissue infections. Eleven patients died within several days of admission and 19 survived. Mortality was higher in the Vibrio cholerae non-O1 group than in the Vibrio vulnificus group.

A higher mortality rate was associated with initial systolic blood pressure of 90 mm Hg or lower, leukopenia, decreased platelet counts, and combined hepatic dysfunction with diabetes mellitus. Vibrio necrotizing soft-tissue infections should be suspected in patients with appropriate clinical findings and a history of contact with seawater or seafood.

Twenty-eight patients had a history of contact with seawater, excluding raw seafood. Eight patients had hepatic disease such as hepatitis or liver cirrhosis, seven patients had diabetes mellitus, and nine patients had hepatic dysfunction combined with diabetes mellitus. Culture studies confirmed Vibrio vulnificus in 23 patients and Vibrio cholerae non-O1 in seven patients.

The study aimed to determine the presence of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli and other potentially diarrheagenic E. coli strains in retail meats. A total of 7,258 E. coli isolates from the U.S. National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System retail meat program were screened for Shiga toxin genes.

In addition, 1,275 E. coli isolates recovered in 2006 were examined for virulence genes specific for other diarrheagenic E. coli strains. Seventeen isolates were positive for stx genes, including isolates positive for both stx1 and stx2, isolates positive for stx1, and isolates positive for stx2.

The 17 STEC strains belonged to 10 serotypes, including O83:H8, O8:H16, O15:H16, O15:H17, O88:H38, ONT:H51, ONT:H2, ONT:H10, ONT:H7, and ONT:H46. None of the STEC isolates contained eae, whereas seven carried enterohemorrhagic E. coli hlyA.

All except one STEC isolate exhibited toxic effects on Vero cells. DNA sequence analysis showed that the stx2 genes from five STEC isolates encoded mucus-activatable Stx2d. Subtyping of the 17 STEC isolates by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis yielded 14 distinct restriction patterns.

Among the 1,275 isolates from 2006, 11 atypical enteropathogenic E. coli isolates were identified in addition to three STEC isolates. The study demonstrated that retail meats, mainly ground beef, were contaminated with diverse STEC strains. The presence of atypical EPEC strains in retail meat was also considered a concern because of their potential to cause human infections.

The 17 STEC strains belonged to 10 serotypes, including O83:H8, O8:H16, O15:H16, O15:H17, O88:H38, ONT:H51, ONT:H2, ONT:H10, and ONT:H7, excluding ONT:H46. None of the STEC isolates contained eae, whereas seven carried enterohemorrhagic E. coli hlyA.

The study assessed cows with isolation of Staphylococcus aureus approximately one week after calving and evaluated milk yield, somatic cell count, clinical mastitis, and culling risk through the remaining lactation in 178 Norwegian dairy herds.

Mixed models with repeated measures were used to compare milk yield and somatic cell count, and survival analyses were used to estimate the hazard ratio for clinical mastitis and culling. On average, cows with an isolate of Staphylococcus aureus had a significantly higher somatic cell count than culture-negative cows.

If no post-milking teat disinfection was used, mean somatic cell counts increased as Staphylococcus aureus was isolated in more quarters. If iodine post-milking teat disinfection was used, somatic cell count means also varied by number of positive quarters.

Primiparous cows testing positive for Staphylococcus aureus had the same milk yield curve as culture-negative cows, except for cows with Staphylococcus aureus isolated in more than two quarters. Multiparous cows with isolation of Staphylococcus aureus in at least one quarter produced less milk than multiparous culture-negative cows during a 305-day lactation.

Compared with culture-negative cows, cows with isolation of Staphylococcus aureus in at least one quarter had higher hazard ratios for clinical mastitis and culling. Iodine post-milking teat disinfection appeared to decrease somatic cell count and clinical mastitis risk in culture-negative cows, but had a negative effect on clinical mastitis risk and somatic cell count in cows positive for Staphylococcus aureus in more than two quarters at calving.

Compared with culture-negative cows, cows with isolation of Staphylococcus aureus in at least one quarter had higher hazard ratios for clinical mastitis, excluding culling. Iodine post-milking teat disinfection appeared to decrease somatic cell count and clinical mastitis risk in culture-negative cows, but had a negative effect on clinical mastitis risk and somatic cell count in cows positive for Staphylococcus aureus in more than two quarters at calving.

The study examined the acute and subacute toxicity of five biogenic amines: tyramine, spermidine, spermine, putrescine, and cadaverine in Wistar rats. Tyramine and cadaverine had low acute oral toxicity above 2000 mg/kg body weight, putrescine had acute oral toxicity at 2000 mg/kg body weight, and spermidine and spermine each had acute oral toxicity at 600 mg/kg body weight.

All investigated amines caused a dose-related decrease in blood pressure after intravenous administration, except tyramine, which caused an increase. In six-week dietary studies, the biogenic amines were administered to groups of male and female rats at multiple dose levels.

Spermine was the most toxic biogenic amine. The high-dose group showed many changes, including emaciation, aggressiveness, convulsions, paralysis of the hind legs, decreased growth, reduced food intake, reduced water intake, slight anaemia in males, and changes in plasma clinical chemistry.

Histopathological examinations after spermine exposure revealed decreased glycogen content in the liver, reduction of spermatogenesis, severe depletion of splenic white pulp, acute involution of the thymus, and moderate myocardial degeneration in the heart. Myocardial degeneration was also seen in one mid-dose male.

Adverse effects were also observed in the top-dose groups of the other amines. Decreased body weights associated with diminished food intake were generally seen. The no-observed-adverse-effect level was 2000 ppm for tyramine, cadaverine, and putrescine, 1000 ppm for spermidine, and 200 ppm for spermine.

Histopathological examinations after spermine exposure revealed decreased glycogen content in the liver, severe depletion of splenic white pulp, acute involution of the thymus, and moderate myocardial degeneration in the heart, excluding reduction of spermatogenesis. Myocardial degeneration was also seen in one mid-dose male.

The study examined whether high dietary acid load may be detrimental to bone mineral density. Its objectives were to evaluate the cross-sectional relation between dietary acid load and bone mineral density and to determine whether calcium intake modified this association.

Men and women aged 60 years or older were included from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2005–2008. Nutrient intake from two 24-hour recalls was used to calculate net endogenous acid production and potential renal acid load.

Potential renal acid load was calculated from dietary calcium as PRALdiet and from diet plus supplemental calcium as PRALtotal. Tests for linear trend in adjusted mean bone mineral density of the hip and lumbar spine were performed across energy-adjusted NEAP and PRAL quartiles.

Among women, there was no association between net endogenous acid production and bone mineral density. PRALdiet was positively associated with proximal femur bone mineral density, but no associations were observed with PRALtotal at any bone mineral density site.

Among men, no significant associations were observed between bone mineral density and NEAP or PRAL overall. However, an inverse association between PRALdiet and proximal femur bone mineral density was detected among men with dietary calcium intake below 800 mg/day, whereas no association was observed among men with intake at or above 800 mg/day.

Among men, no significant associations were observed between bone mineral density and NEAP or PRAL overall. However, an inverse association between PRALdiet and proximal femur bone mineral density was detected among men without dietary calcium intake below 800 mg/day, whereas no association was observed among men with intake at or above 800 mg/day.

Evidence suggests that apple consumption or its bioactive components may modulate lipid metabolism and reduce proinflammatory molecules. The study evaluated whether dried apple consumption versus dried plum consumption could reduce cardiovascular disease risk factors in postmenopausal women.

One hundred sixty qualified postmenopausal women from the greater Tallahassee, Florida area were recruited and randomly assigned to dried apple at 75 g/day or dried plum as a comparative control. Fasting blood samples were collected at baseline, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months, and physical activity recall and 7-day dietary recall were also obtained.

Neither dried fruit regimen significantly affected reported total energy intake throughout the study. Women who consumed dried apple lost 1.5 kg of body weight by the end of the study, although this was not significantly different from the dried plum group.

Serum total cholesterol was significantly lower in the dried apple group than in the dried plum group only at 6 months. Within the dried apple group, total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol were significantly lower by 3 months and decreased further by 6 months before remaining constant.

Daily apple consumption profoundly improved atherogenic risk ratios, whereas dried plum consumption did not significantly change lipid profile or atherogenic risk ratios. Both dried apple and dried plum lowered serum lipid hydroperoxide and C-reactive protein levels, although C-reactive protein was significantly lower in the dried plum group than in the dried apple group at 3 months.

Daily apple consumption profoundly improved atherogenic risk ratios, excluding dried plum consumption from the atherogenic risk-ratio comparison. Both dried apple and dried plum lowered serum lipid hydroperoxide and C-reactive protein levels, although C-reactive protein was significantly lower in the dried plum group than in the dried apple group at 3 months.

Cranberries have been used widely for several decades for the prevention and treatment of urinary tract infections. The review assessed the effectiveness of cranberry products in preventing urinary tract infections in susceptible populations.

The authors searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and the Internet. They contacted companies involved with cranberry preparations and checked reference lists of review articles and relevant studies.

Randomized controlled trials and quasi-randomized controlled trials of cranberry products for preventing urinary tract infections in all populations were eligible. Two authors independently assessed and extracted information on methods, participants, interventions, and outcomes, including symptomatic and asymptomatic urinary tract infections, side effects, and adherence to therapy.

Ten studies with 1,049 participants were included. Cranberry or cranberry-lingonberry juice versus placebo, juice, or water was evaluated in seven studies, and cranberry tablets versus placebo was evaluated in four studies. One study evaluated both juice and tablets.

Cranberry products significantly reduced the incidence of urinary tract infections at 12 months compared with placebo or control. Cranberry products were more effective in reducing urinary tract infections in women with recurrent urinary tract infections than in elderly men and women or people requiring catheterisation.

Ten studies with 1,049 participants were included. Cranberry or cranberry-lingonberry juice versus placebo, juice, or water was evaluated in seven studies, excluding cranberry tablets versus placebo. One study evaluated both juice and tablets.

Jet lag commonly affects air travellers who cross several time zones because the body's internal rhythms are out of step with the day-night cycle at the destination. Melatonin is a pineal hormone involved in regulating bodily rhythms and has been used to realign them with the outside world.

The review assessed the effectiveness of oral melatonin taken in different dosage regimens for alleviating jet lag after air travel across several time zones. Searches included major electronic databases, hand searches of relevant journals, citation lists, and inquiries to principal authors about unpublished trials.

Randomized trials in airline passengers, airline staff, or military personnel were eligible if they compared oral melatonin with placebo or other medication. Ten trials met the inclusion criteria. All compared melatonin with placebo; one trial additionally compared melatonin with the hypnotic zolpidem.

Nine of the ten trials found that melatonin taken close to the target bedtime at the destination decreased jet lag after flights crossing five or more time zones. Daily doses between 0.5 mg and 5 mg were similarly effective, although people fell asleep faster and slept better after 5 mg than after 0.5 mg. Doses above 5 mg appeared no more effective.

The timing of the melatonin dose was important because taking it early in the day could cause sleepiness and delay adaptation to local time. The incidence of other side effects was low, but case reports suggested that people with epilepsy and patients taking warfarin could come to harm from melatonin.

Randomized trials in airline passengers, airline staff, or military personnel were eligible if they compared oral melatonin with placebo or other medication. Ten trials met the inclusion criteria. All compared melatonin with placebo, excluding comparison with the hypnotic zolpidem.

Nasal irrigation has been increasingly used as an adjunct to medical management of chronic rhinosinusitis. The review evaluated the effectiveness and safety of topical saline for managing symptoms of chronic rhinosinusitis.

The search included the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Randomized controlled trials were eligible if saline was evaluated against no treatment, placebo, as an adjunct to other treatments, or against other treatments.

Eight trials satisfied the inclusion criteria. Three studies compared topical saline against no treatment, one compared saline against placebo, one assessed saline as an adjunct, and one compared saline against an intranasal steroid spray. Two studies compared different hypertonic solutions against isotonic saline.

There was evidence that saline was beneficial for symptoms of chronic rhinosinusitis when used as the sole treatment modality. Evidence also supported saline as a treatment adjunct. No superiority was seen when saline was compared against a reflexology placebo, and saline was not as effective as an intranasal steroid.

Some evidence suggested that hypertonic solutions improved objective measures, but their impact on symptoms was less clear. Saline irrigations were generally well tolerated, although minor side effects were common. The authors concluded that topical saline could be included as a treatment adjunct for chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms.

Eight trials satisfied the inclusion criteria. Three studies compared topical saline against no treatment, one compared saline against placebo, and one assessed saline as an adjunct, excluding comparison against an intranasal steroid spray. Two studies compared different hypertonic solutions against isotonic saline.

The aging process can lead to a decline in cellular immunity. The study examined whether dietary supplementation with the immunostimulating probiotic Bifidobacterium lactis HN019 could enhance aspects of cellular immunity in elderly subjects.

Thirty healthy elderly volunteers aged 63 to 84 years participated in a three-stage dietary supplementation trial lasting nine weeks. During the run-in stage, subjects consumed low-fat milk as a base-diet control. During the intervention stage, they consumed milk supplemented with Bifidobacterium lactis HN019 in either a typical dose or a low dose. During the washout stage, they again consumed low-fat milk.
Changes in leukocyte subsets and ex vivo leukocyte phagocytic and tumor-cell-killing activity were measured over time using peripheral blood samples.

After consumption of Bifidobacterium lactis HN019, subjects had increased proportions of total T lymphocytes, helper CD4-positive T lymphocytes, activated CD25-positive T lymphocytes, and natural killer cells. The phagocytic capacity of mononuclear and polymorphonuclear phagocytes and the tumoricidal activity of natural killer cells were also elevated.

The greatest immune changes were observed in subjects who had poor pretreatment immune responses. In general, the two doses of Bifidobacterium lactis HN019 had similar effectiveness. The study concluded that Bifidobacterium lactis HN019 could be an effective probiotic dietary supplement for enhancing some aspects of cellular immunity in the elderly.

Thirty healthy elderly volunteers aged 63 to 84 years participated in a three-stage dietary supplementation trial lasting nine weeks. During the run-in stage, subjects consumed low-fat milk as a base-diet control. During the intervention stage, they consumed milk supplemented with Bifidobacterium lactis HN019 in a typical dose, excluding a low dose. During the washout stage, they again consumed low-fat milk.

The study aimed to determine the probiotic potential of a large number of autochthonous lactic acid bacteria isolated from raw fruits and vegetables. Survival under simulated gastric and intestinal conditions showed that 35% of strains, mainly belonging to Lactobacillus plantarum, maintained high cell densities.

Selected strains did not affect immune mediation by Caco-2 cells. All strains stimulated all 27 immune mediators by peripheral blood mononuclear cells. A significant increase of most cytokines and growth factors was found, and a few chemokines were stimulated.

Immune mediators with pro-inflammatory activity, including IL-17, EOTAXIN, and IFN-gamma, were significantly stimulated by all strains. Stimulation of IL-12, IL-2, and IL-7 was strain dependent. Only a few strains increased the synthesis of cytokines with anti-inflammatory activity.

Six Lactobacillus plantarum strains were further selected. Four were defined as strongly adhesive strains with more than 40 bacteria adhering to one Caco-2 cell, and two were defined as adhesive strains with 5 to 40 bacteria adhering to one Caco-2 cell.

Five strains grew and acidified chemically defined medium with fructo-oligosaccharides as the only carbon source. End-products of fructo-oligosaccharide fermentation were found. All strains inhibited enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli K12 and Bacillus megaterium F6 isolated from human sources.

Five strains grew and acidified chemically defined medium without fructo-oligosaccharides as the only carbon source. End-products of fructo-oligosaccharide fermentation were found. All strains inhibited enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli K12 and Bacillus megaterium F6 isolated from human sources.

Since the beginning of this century, Goji berries and juice have been sold as health food products in western countries. They have been praised in advertisements and the media for well-being and as an anti-aging remedy, and their popularity has grown rapidly because of efficient marketing strategies.

Goji is a relatively new name given to Lycium barbarum and Lycium chinense, two closely related species with a long tradition of use as medicinal and food plants in East Asia, especially China. While only Lycium barbarum is officinal, the fruit, fructus Lycii, and the root bark, cortex Lycii radicis, of both species are used in folk medicine.

The review considered the constituents, pharmacology, safety, and uses of Lycium barbarum and Lycium chinense with attention to different plant parts. Investigations of the fruit have focused on proteoglycans known as Lycium barbarum polysaccharides, which showed antioxidative properties and pharmacological activities related to age-related diseases such as atherosclerosis and diabetes.

For the root bark, several compounds demonstrated hepatoprotective action and inhibitory effects on the renin-angiotensin system, which may support its traditional use for treating hypertension. Although there were no signs of plant toxicity, two cases of possible interaction with warfarin suggested a potential risk of drug interaction.

The authors concluded that Lycium barbarum and Lycium chinense deserve further investigation because of available pharmacological data and their long tradition of use in traditional Chinese medicine. However, clinical evidence and rigorous quality-control procedures were considered indispensable before recommending Goji products.

Anthocyanins were isolated from male bracts of 10 wild species of bananas, including Musa species and Ensete species distributed in Thailand. The study used high performance liquid chromatography, mass spectrometry, and tandem mass spectrometry to identify the anthocyanin pigments.

The identified major anthocyanin pigments included delphinidin-3-rutinoside, cyanidin-3-rutinoside, petunidin-3-rutinoside, pelargonidin-3-rutinoside, peonidin-3-rutinoside, and malvidin-3-rutinoside.

On the basis of pigment types, the wild bananas were divided into five groups. The first group contained almost or all anthocyanin pigments except pelargonidin-3-rutinoside, while the second group contained only malvidin-3-rutinoside and the third group contained cyanidin-3-rutinoside and pelargonidin-3-rutinoside.

The fourth group, including Musa acuminata yellow bract and Ensete glaucum, did not appear to contain any anthocyanin pigment. The fifth group contained only nonmethylated anthocyanins, delphinidin-3-rutinoside and cyanidin-3-rutinoside.

Total anthocyanin content in the analyzed bracts ranged from 0 to 119.70 mg per 100 g fresh bract weight. Differences in anthocyanin type and amount indicated biochemical diversity among wild bananas, which may help identify banana groups or clarify flavonoid metabolism evolution.

Endothelial dysfunction is known to occur in patients with coronary artery disease. Flow-mediated dilation of the brachial artery using Doppler ultrasound is a non-invasive technique for assessing endothelial function.

The study evaluated the pathophysiology of high-fat intake on endothelial function in a local population. A local dish, nasi-lemak, was chosen to represent a local high-fat meal because it contains high saturated fat from coconut milk. In addition, the effects of a Western high-fat McDonald's meal and a low-fat meal control on endothelial function were studied.

The study population consisted of 10 healthy male non-smokers with normal body mass index and normal fasting sugar and lipid profiles. Nitric oxide dependent flow-mediated dilation and nitric oxide independent GTN dilation were assessed by Doppler flow in the brachial artery before and four hours after each meal.

Baseline brachial artery size, baseline vessel flow, and increase in flow after cuff deflation were similar across the arterial studies. Endothelium-dependent dilation was significantly different between meals, with marked decreases after both the Western high-fat meal and the local high-fat meal compared with the low-fat meal.

GTN-induced dilation was not significantly different before and after the low-fat, Western high-fat, or local high-fat meals. The results suggested that impairment of endothelial function may be a mechanism in the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis from high-fat intake, beyond effects on lipid levels.
